title: Periodic Classification and Trends
scope_note: School-level formative periodic classification retained; quantitative subshell ionisation trends explicitly ENRICHMENT
introduction: The periodic table is a scientific model that organises evidence and makes predictions. We start with how historical patterns were tested, then use proton number and outer-electron structure to infer group behaviour, formulae and the limitations of broad trends. An optional advanced chapter examines the exceptions rather than pretending that every arrow is absolute.

subtopics.title: Dobereiner, Newlands and Mendeleev classification
subtopics.entry_question: How did nineteenth-century chemists see a pattern in elements before protons were even known?
core1a_paragraphs: Scientific classification compresses many observations into a predictive model. Döbereiner grouped certain similar elements into triads with approximately related atomic masses. Newlands recognised approximate repetitions after every eighth element among lighter elements, but this pattern did not accommodate all known elements.

Mendeleev used atomic masses and chemical properties to organise elements. A major strength was that he left gaps and predicted properties for not-yet-discovered elements. Successful predictions offered evidence that the periodic pattern captured something real, while some element orderings remained problematic.

A historical model should be judged against the evidence and knowledge available at the time. Its failures are scientifically important: they show why atomic number, rather than atomic mass, later became the organising variable.
subtopics.representation: Show a chronological comparison table: triads, octaves, Mendeleev periodic table, modern atomic-number table. Columns: organising variable, successful prediction, observed limitation.

worked_example.problem: In a sample Döbereiner-type triad, first/third atomic masses are 7 and 39. Estimate middle mass by arithmetic mean.
steps: Historical triad heuristic compares middle mass with average of outside members.
Compare with approximate sodium atomic mass near 23.
This is a pattern observation, not a universally valid law for all triads.
worked_example.check: Check the chemical similarity and limitations rather than treating mean as proof.

misconception.wrong: A successful numerical average alone proves three elements share chemical properties.
misconception.why: Chemical behaviour and periodic position provide independent evidence; mass averages can occur by coincidence.
misconception.repair: Use property patterns and predictive accuracy as well as a numerical match.

subtopics.title: Modern periodic law and table organisation
subtopics.entry_question: If argon has greater relative atomic mass than potassium, why does argon still come first in the modern periodic table?
core1a_paragraphs: The modern periodic law states that physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Atomic number Z counts protons. It is more fundamental to element identity than an average isotopic atomic mass.

Arranging elements in increasing Z organises them so that valence electronic patterns repeat. Periods represent progressive filling patterns and groups collect elements with related outer-electron features and chemical behaviour.

The table is not simply a list of elements sorted by a single property. Its shape also reflects quantum electronic structure; the school-level pattern explains main-group positions without requiring complete orbital theory.
subtopics.representation: Compare Ar: Z18, relative atomic mass about39.95 and K: Z19, about39.10. Place Ar before K by Z, not mass.

worked_example.problem: Given Argon Z=18 and potassium Z=19, choose their order even if tabulated masses differ.

Argon has Z18, potassium Z19.
Place Ar before K.

subtopics.title: Groups, periods and valence patterns
subtopics.entry_question: Why do lithium and sodium tend to form +1 ions, while magnesium often forms +2?
core1a_paragraphs: Elements in a main-group column share a characteristic outer-electron pattern. Lithium has 2,1 and sodium has 2,8,1; both have one outer electron in a simple shell model. Magnesium 2,8,2 has two outer electrons.

Period number for these simple main-group examples corresponds to the highest occupied shell. Across period 3 from Na to Ar, valence electron count increases and chemical behaviour changes progressively.
Group patterns support predictions about common valency and types of compounds. They are starting points, not guarantees of every oxidation state or reaction under every condition.
subtopics.representation: A mini periodic grid shows Na/Mg/Al/Si/P/S/Cl/Ar across period 3 and Li directly above Na. Annotate outer-shell counts without confusing them with full configurations.

worked_example.problem: Element X has shell configuration 2,8,2. Predict period and group and likely simple ion charge.
steps: Three occupied shells imply period 3.
Two outer electrons place a main-group element in group 2.
It may lose two electrons in simple ionic compounds.
The common cation charge is +2; X is magnesium.

misconception.wrong: An element in period 3 must have three valence electrons.
misconception.why: Period tracks occupied shell index, not outer electron count.
misconception.repair: Count shells and outer electrons separately.

subtopics.title: Metallic and nonmetallic trends
subtopics.entry_question: Why does metallic character generally decrease when moving across a period, yet increase down some groups?
core1a_paragraphs: Metallic behaviour is associated with the ease of losing electrons, though it is not a single direct measured quantity. Across a main-group period, increasing nuclear charge without another main shell tends to increase attraction for valence electrons, making simple electron loss less favourable.

Down a main group such as the alkali metals, a new outer shell and shielding generally place the valence electron farther from the nucleus, often making its removal easier despite increased total nuclear charge.

These are qualitative trends with domain limits. Atomic size, ionisation energies, electron interactions and chemical environments all contribute; it is unscientific to claim each property is strictly monotonic for every element.
subtopics.representation: Use two arrows on a mini periodic table: main-group metallic tendency decreases across toward the right, generally increases down group 1. Label them 'tendencies' not absolute formulas.

worked_example.problem: Between Na and K, which has its outer electron in a higher principal shell?
steps: Na neutral configuration 2,8,1 has outer shell n3.
K neutral configuration is 2,8,8,1, outer shell n4 in school representation.
K has outer electron farther out on average with more shielding.
This supports its tendency to lose an electron more readily.
worked_example.check: Compare main-group position and outer-shell level, not only Z.

misconception.wrong: More protons automatically mean valence electrons are harder to remove in all comparisons.
misconception.why: Additional shells and shielding change the effective attraction.
misconception.repair: Compare shell levels and screening before predicting.

subtopics.title: Chemical prediction from table position
subtopics.entry_question: Can we use an element's periodic position to predict its compounds without knowing its name?
core1a_paragraphs: A periodic table position summarises atomic number and electron structure. For many main-group elements it supports predictions of common ion charges and simple formulae. A group-1 element often gives +1; a group-2 element gives +2; group-17 halogens often give −1.

These predictions need charge balance, chemical context and knowledge of whether the proposed bond type is reasonable. A formula based solely on group number may be invalid for a covalent compound or a multiple-valence transition metal.

Using an unknown element symbol X is scientifically useful: the student must derive its valence behaviour rather than recall a memorised compound. The check is total charge and consistency with shell patterns.
subtopics.representation: A decision tree begins group/period clues → valence pattern → likely charge/bond model → formula → charge/evidence check. Keep periodic position and formula as separate operations.

worked_example.problem: Unknown X is group 2 and unknown Y is a typical group 17 element. Propose simple neutral formula.
steps: Group2 model gives cation X²⁺.
Group17 halogen model gives anion Y⁻.
Total neutrality requires one X with two Y.
Formula is XY₂.
worked_example.result: XY₂ under the simple ionic charge model.
worked_example.check: One X²⁺ and two Y⁻ give total charge +2 + 2(−1)=0, so the simplest empirical formula is XY₂.

misconception.wrong: A group number directly supplies a formula subscript with no chemical reasoning.
misconception.why: Formulas encode charges or covalent valence, not periodic coordinates.

subtopics.title: Quantitative periodic trends and exceptions (enrichment)
subtopics.entry_question: Does increasing nuclear charge always make an electron harder to remove from a neutral atom?
core1a_paragraphs: First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom in its ground state. Across a main-group period, it often increases because electrons experience greater effective nuclear attraction.

The trend has local exceptions. For example, B has a lower first ionisation energy than Be because B's electron removed is from a higher-energy 2p subshell rather than Be's filled 2s subshell; O is lower than N because paired 2p electrons increase repulsion relative to N's half-filled 2p set.

These explanations require a subshell model beyond compulsory secondary content. They are useful D4 enrichment only when the student has already learned the relevant electron configurations and energetic assumptions.
Electronegativity, electron affinity and ionisation energy are not interchangeable concepts. A single periodic arrow cannot replace their distinct definitions.
subtopics.representation: Sketch qualitative first-ionisation-energy trend across period2 with local dips at B and O, label it 'enrichment' and identify subshell-pairing causes.

worked_example.problem: Compare qualitatively the first ionisation energies of Be (1s²2s²) and B (1s²2s²2p¹).
steps: Identify the electron that would be removed from each neutral atom.
Be loses a 2s electron; B loses its 2p electron.
A 2p electron is generally higher in energy and easier to remove in this comparison.
Therefore B's first ionisation energy is slightly lower than Be's despite larger Z.
worked_example.result: First IE(B) < first IE(Be), a local exception.
worked_example.check: The model must explain an energy effect, not merely invoke a remembered exception.

misconception.wrong: Ionisation energy must rise perfectly at every step across a period.
misconception.why: Subshell energies and electron pairing can change the local trend.
misconception.repair: Compare the electron actually removed and its orbital/repulsion environment.
